title: Compatibility tiers and change-criticality policy for the serving runtime
creator: Ava Chen
description:
Problem: We lack a concise, machine-actionable policy that maps types of changes to required review gates, rollout paths, and deprecation windows for the runtime. This causes ad-hoc decisions at release time and increases risk of regressions for customers on Dedicated/LTS channels.

Goal: Define 'compatibility tiers' and a 'change-criticality' matrix that (1) standardizes whether a change is allowed on LTS/minor/patch, (2) describes required CI/QA gating, (3) prescribes rollout behavior and automated rollback triggers, and (4) defines tooling to detect and enforce policy during PR and release automation.
acceptance_criteria:
1) A documented compatibility tier taxonomy (Tier A..D) exists and is agreed by Release Eng, Runtime, and Platform PMs.
2) A change-criticality matrix exists mapping code-change patterns to gates (unit tests, compat tests, manual review, SRE signoff).
3) CI runs a new 'compat-check' that classifies PRs and annotates required reviewers/approval labels automatically.
4) Release pipeline enforces gates for LTS/minor/major according to the matrix.
5) Console shows a migration checklist when customers request runtime upgrades that include any Tier B+ changes.
technical_notes:
Proposed taxonomy:
- Tier A (Binary & protocol stable): Calling surface, on-disk KV format, network protocol compatibility. Changes allowed only in major; only non-functional patches on minor/patch.
- Tier B (Public API behavior): REST/GRPC shape, JSON output fields, header semantics. Deprecations allowed with 2 release windows (>= 90 days).
- Tier C (Runtime heuristics & scheduling): Batching/kernels/scheduling defaults that can affect performance but not correctness. Allowed on minor with canary and rollback policy.
- Tier D (Internal refactors): Internal module boundaries, logging, code cleanup. Allowed on patch if covered by tests.

Change-criticality levels: Low/Medium/High/Critical mapped to automated tests, required reviewers, and rollout strategy. Example mapping: Low=unit tests, auto-merge; Medium=integration + compat suite + 1 PM review; High=compat suite + SRE + canary; Critical=blocker incident path, require oncall & SE signoff.

Compat-check implementation: Static PR heuristics plus a set of runtime compatibility tests (compat-suite) that run against pinned models + synthetic traffic. The compat-check will output a classification label and add a GitHub PR comment with checklist and required approvals.

Deprecation headers and telemetry: Add X-Redwood-Deprecated: v<version> header on responses, and deprecation events emitted to metrics pipeline (deprecated_api.used). Deprecation windows are configured per tier; example: Tier B = 90-180 days, Tier A = >180 days with formal migration support.

Rollout gates: local unit -> integration -> compat-suite -> 1% canary (48h) -> 10% canary (24h) -> staged rollout (25/50/100). Automatic rollback whenever: error_rate increase > 0.3% absolute or 50% relative for p95+ latency or any regression in regression-eval prompt sets.

Upgrade tooling: 'runtime-migrate' CLI that queries service version, shows diff of deprecated APIs, runs a simulated traffic test against a sandboxed upgrade, and generates a customer-facing migration plan. Console UI will surface migration blockers and allow scheduling a managed upgrade with snapshot and rollback options.
rollout_plan:
- Week 1: Align taxonomy with Runtime and Platform leads; socialise in eng-all.
- Week 2: Implement compat-check prototype as GitHub Action + PR labeler.
- Week 3: Add compat-suite tests to CI and wire automatic classification.
- Week 4: Integrate gating into release pipeline for non-LTS channels.
- Week 5: Pilot LTS gating on a small internal LTS branch and run a staged canary.
- Week 6: Console migration checklist and runtime-migrate beta.

Fallbacks: If compat-suite is flaky, we will fall back to manual SRE signoff for high-criticality changes and postpone minor release until flakes fixed.
